fixes.explanation: Jacob says, “…my honesty will testify for me when you come to check on my wages in the future.” He's inviting Laban to come look for himself. Then he spells out what would count against him: goats that are not speckled or spotted, or lambs that are not dark-colored, “will be considered stolen.” That's a man leaving the cookie jar open and saying, “Count 'em.”

Jacob, Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), goes to Laban and says, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” He's asking to go home, not to set up shop where he is. The request is about leaving, and Laban is the one who has to answer it.

Staying close by isn't what Jacob asks. He says, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” A house next door would be a very short trip for a man talking about going home. The request points toward leaving.

I can see why you'd think it, but Jacob says the opposite. He tells Laban, “Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way.” He's asking for his wives and children, so they're part of the request. Leaving them behind would be a strange way to ask for them.

Right, his family is part of the request. Jacob says, “Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way.” He wants his wives and children given to him, not left with Laban. This family is not getting left at the rest stop, friend.

Laban doesn't say anything about a warning. He says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” Blessing is the word on the table, and it's tied to Jacob. A warning never comes up.

Nothing in Laban's words is about a test. He says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” Then he asks, “If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay.” Laban sounds like a man who already read the results, and I think he liked them.

Jacob asks for “…every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat.” Then he says, “These will be my wages.” He's naming animals by their markings and color. That's his whole offer, and it comes with one condition.

Kindness is a fine thing, but it's not what Jacob names. He says, “…my honesty will testify for me…” Then he names what would be considered stolen: goats that are not speckled or spotted, and lambs that are not dark-colored. Honesty is the word he picks for that.

Laban removes the animals “…that very day” and places them “…under the care of his sons.” Those are Laban's own sons, not Jacob's. So the animals Jacob named are now with someone else. Laban doesn't waste a minute, and I think that tells you something.

Jacob's sons aren't the ones watching them. The text says Laban placed the animals under the care of his sons. That means Laban's own household takes charge. Watch the names here, because it's easy to mix up whose sons are whose.

Leah and Rachel are Jacob's wives (Genesis 29:23, 28), but they aren't who Laban picks. The text says he put the animals under the care of his sons. So the animals go to Laban's sons. Leah and Rachel aren't part of this handoff.

Jacob takes fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees and peels the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” So what shows is white wood. A peeled branch looks very different from a bark-covered one, and that's what he sets out.
No sap in this verse. The text says Jacob peeled the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” What the verse names is white wood. Green sap never shows up.

That's the wrong color. Peel those branches and “…the white inner wood of the branches” is what shows. Dark wood isn't in the verse. Jacob was holding branches that looked pale where the bark came off.

Jacob sets the peeled branches “…in the watering troughs in front of the flocks coming in to drink.” The branches go right where the flocks come to drink. I think Jacob picked that spot with care. Location, location, location.

Not the open fields. The verse says Jacob set the peeled branches “…in the watering troughs in front of the flocks coming in to drink.” The branches go where the flocks come to drink. Jacob wasn't leaving them lying around the pasture.

The text says the flocks mated in front of the branches and “…bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted.” That's what came out of it. Genesis tells us what happened and doesn't explain why. I think Jacob was watching those lambs and kids closely.

They came out marked. The flocks “…bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted.” Plain ones aren't what the verse reports. Genesis just tells us what happened, and I bet Jacob took a good long look.

Right, he keeps them apart. The text says Jacob “…set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban’s animals.” His animals stay separate from Laban's. There's no mixing the two groups together.
Thirsty isn't the word. The verse says, “…if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” Thirst never comes up there. Weak is the word that decides it.

Young isn't the word. The verse says, “…if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” Strength is what the text goes by here. Age doesn't come up, and a strong animal gets the branches while a weak one doesn't.

Debt isn't in the picture. The text says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He owned large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. That's a long list of things, and a tab owed to Laban isn't on it.
